techniques.comment: The Russian Empire led the Nokhchi who survived the destruction of an aul away as captives into its own territory. General Yermolov himself writes in his “Notes” that women and children “were taken prisoner numbering up to one hundred and forty”(Citation: Записки А.П. Ермолова. 1798-1826 гг. 1991), and the imperial historian Potto confirms this(Citation: Кавказская война. В 5 томах. Том 2. Ермоловское время 2007). Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that during the crossing of the captives over the Terek, 46 captured girls, “not wishing to endure abuse in captivity,” perished, “dragging their guards with them into the turbulent river”(Citation: Чеченцы в Русско-Кавказской войне 1998).

The overseers appointed by the empire over the auls (the pristavs), within the amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line (a chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), systematically robbed the inhabitants of the seized auls of Chechnya under the guise of collections. The imperial historian Yurov described the mechanism - the pristavs lived off exactions, since "not all pristavs received a salary": from the Chechens, "under the pretext of collecting tributes and fines, the best weapons were taken away, and other entirely harmless but valuable articles of everyday use; it happened that people innocent of anything were arrested at the prompting of simple and often ill-intentioned interpreters... and during expeditions forced collections were permitted"(Citation: 1840, 1841 и 1842-й годы на Кавказе 1886). The empire knew and would not listen: the historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write from archival documents that two Chechen elders brought to the Kabardian prince Bekovich-Cherkassky, who served the empire and was influential on the Terek river, "a petition drawn up on behalf of many Chechens, in which they complain of the oppressions and injustices of major-general Pullo" - the prince refused to accept the petition(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005); according to Yurov, the Chechens "had prepared a petition against him, but did not dare to set it in motion for fear that this general would remain their superior as before"(Citation: 1840, 1841 и 1842-й годы на Кавказе 1886). The empire's survey "The Region in Political and Military Respects", sent by the empire's Minister of War Chernyshev to general Neidhardt, who soon headed the empire's troops in the Caucasus, on 2 April 1842, summed it up: "taking advantage of the abuses, the exactions and the indignation arising from the confiscation of weapons, Shamil little by little stirred all Chechnya to revolt" (Shamil - imam, leader of the resistance of the highlanders of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest)(Citation: Кавказские войны и имамат Шамиля 2009).

The seizure and incorporation into the empire of Right-Bank Ukraine, Volhynia, and Podillia: Russia received "the Kyiv, Bratslav, and Podillia voivodeships and the eastern half of the Volhynian voivodeship," and under the third partition – "the western part of the Volhynian voivodeship, the western parts of the Kholm land and the Belz voivodeship"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 8 2011).

The Russian Empire condemned the Nokhchi inhabitants to famine by ravaging their villages, crops, and stores. Historian D. A. Khozhaev writes that after Yermolov's campaign, deprived of shelter and food, «people were dying of hunger, cold, and disease»(Citation: Чеченцы в Русско-Кавказской войне 1998).

The Russian Empire bought the loyalty of Nokhchi elders in order to use them to bring recalcitrant villages into subjecthood. The commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, General Gudovich, instructed the Andreyevo elder Hadji-Redjeb to incline the villages “into submission and subjecthood,” and assigned a salary to the Chechen uzden Bik-Bulat — “I persuaded the Chechen uzden Bik-Bulat… to whom I said… a salary of 300 r. in silver per year”; for winning over the remaining villages, “about 3,000 r. in silver for bringing them into loyal subjecthood” was allocated(Citation: Акты собранные Кавказскою археографическою комиссиею. Том III (1806-1809) 1869). The same bribery, from the Nokhchi side, is recorded by the historian D. A. Khozhaev: through the intermediary Hadji-Redjeb, in the name of the commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, General Gudovich, the very head of the Chechen resistance, Beibulat Taimiev, was won over and took “an oath of fidelity of subjecthood to Russia,” while Hadji-Redjeb asked the generals for another 3000 rubles in silver “for bringing the remaining unpacified Chechen villages into loyal subjecthood”(Citation: Чеченцы в Русско-Кавказской войне 1998).

On 29 June 1919 the central organ of the colonial administration of Ukraine (the VUTsIK) resolved: "To take the most energetic measures to suppress kulak uprisings and the actions of bands, applying the imposition of contributions on rebellious localities and the taking of hostages"; the resolution was signed for the chairman of that organ by Polozov and by its secretary Lapchinsky(Citation: Постановление ВУЦИК о проведении всеобщей мобилизации 1919). Under this resolution it was not the one who rose who had to answer - in money and in hostages - but the whole locality at once.
By the end of the year Moscow fixed the practice for the entire army: on 11 December 1919 Trotsky, war minister of the RSFSR, and Kamenev, commander-in-chief of the RSFSR armed forces, signed secret order No. 579 - every army "undertakes, in its area of operations, to disarm the population with the help of all means at its disposal (agitation, agent intelligence, payment for surrendered weapons in money and in kind, house-to-house searches, fines in money and in kind, collective responsibility, the hostage system, the shooting of culprits, etc., etc.)," and the order, as stated in it, applies "first of all to the armies entering Ukraine"(Citation: Приказ Реввоенсовета Республики № 579 о мерах по борьбе с партизанщиной в Красной Армии 1919).
On 26 July 1919 Skrypnyk, plenipotentiary of the same administration's Defence Council, telegraphed from the area of Zeleny's uprising - in the same words as the orders: "The uprising of the peasants of the Trypillia district has been suppressed... there now remains... the exaction from it of all the expenses borne by the workers' and peasants' state for the suppression," specifying: "It is necessary to carry out the exaction in produce, the exaction from the peasants of the expenses caused by the uprising"(Citation: Телеграмма Н. А. Скрыпника о ликвидации банд Зеленого 1919). In Mohyliv-Podilskyi, which Soviet troops captured on 5 April 1919 without a fight, the town was at once subjected to a forced payment - a telegram to the Bureau of the Ukrainian Press over the signature of Ivanitsky reported: "there is exemplary order in the town, with which even the bourgeoisie is content, despite the imposed contribution of one and a half million"(Citation: Телеграмма из Могилева-Подольского в Бюро украинской печати 1919). The reports of the Special Investigative Commission attached to the Whites' command (the AFSR) record of Odesa: "400 people have been sent to forced labour for non-payment of contributions," and of Izium in Kharkiv province: "eyewitnesses told of the wholesale robbery of families whose relatives had gone over to the 'Kadets'"(Citation: Красный террор в годы гражданской войны 2004).
In Fastiv in Kyiv province the forced payment imposed on the town under the Soviet authority was paid by the Jewish community - Kh. Hofman, an officer of the Editorial Board, the body collecting testimony on the pogroms, recorded: "The entire imposed contribution was paid almost wholly by the Jews, notwithstanding that they are poorer and considerably fewer than the Christians. Many Jews were taken hostage, sat long in prison, many had to leave Fastiv altogether"(Citation: Доклад Х. Гофмана о погромах в м. Фастов Киевской губ. 1919).

In 1836, corps commander Rosen sent covert topographers through Chechnya for the clandestine surveying of the land that had not submitted. In a report to the emperor, Rosen acknowledges: “in 1836, to survey the direct route leading from Kakheti to Chechnya, a topographer was sent who, having crossed the snow ridge, came out onto the Caucasian Line at the fortress of Groznaya, and from there, through Chechnya and the lands of the Kistins and the Didois, returned to Kakheti”; at the same time “I sent from Vladikavkaz Ensign Prince Utsmiev of the Life Guards Grenadier Regiment with a topographer, through Chechnya, to Andia”(Citation: Акты собранные Кавказскою археографическою комиссиею. Том VIII (1831-1837) 1881). Rosen named the method outright: “covert surveys of the lands of the mountaineers hostile to us”(Citation: Акты собранные Кавказскою археографическою комиссиею. Том VIII (1831-1837) 1881).

The deployment of a network of military bases (Novobohorodytska, Kamianyi Zaton) near the Zaporozhian Sich. Under the pretext of protection, Moscow was establishing rigid military control: "The Zaporozhians... put forward the destruction of Kamianyi Zaton as a condition for any oath of allegiance"(Citation: Иван Мазепа и Российская империя. История «предательства» 2011)(Citation: Мазепа 2007).

In 1836, the command of the Russian Caucasus Corps sent the hired preacher Taj ad-Din Mustafin, paid by the treasury, to the Groznaya fortress to undermine the influence of Tashu-Hadji (sheikh, imam of Chechnya in 1834-1836, spiritual and military leader of the Chechen resistance) - a spiritual track running parallel to the punitive military actions against the villages that had harbored Tashu-Hadji (campaign C1158). The goal was stated in the source: "with the aim of undermining the spiritual influence" of Tashu-Hadji "and reducing the effectiveness of the preaching of ghazawat" (ghazawat - the highlanders' war for independence from the Russian conquest)(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005). The agent "had managed to make a trip to the lowland societies of Dagestan" when Tashu-Hadji, by letter, "under threat of death forbade him to appear on Chechen territory"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005); the response is cited by the historian Pokrovsky: "I instruct you that you shall not travel about in these lands without our permission, and if you are not foolish, you should withdraw before harm is done to you"(Citation: Кавказские войны и имамат Шамиля 2009).

The squeezing of the Chechens out of the mountains was built on depriving them of the means of life - and the empire wrote about this openly. Vorontsov, viceroy and commander-in-chief in the Caucasus, reported to Minister of War Chernyshev in an official letter (otnosheniye) of 25 October 1847: "constrained in their means of life, seeing their constant failures, the Chechens waver, and a large number of families are already resettling into our bounds"(Citation: Движение горцев северо-восточного Кавказа в 20-50 гг. XIX века: сборник документов 1959). General Sleptsov, in a report of 4 October 1850, built on this a calculation for the future: the mountain communities, "constrained by our future settlements in the valley, ... will inevitably follow the example of their compatriots" - that is, they too would come down to the fortifications(Citation: Акты собранные Кавказскою археографическою комиссиею. Том X (1844-1854) 1885).

In 1836, the command of the Russian Caucasus Corps under General Rozen established under its own control the post of spiritual leader of all the Sunnis of the Caucasus, and appointed to it the hired Kazan efendi (Muslim theologian) Taj ad-Din Mustafin, maintained at the treasury's expense - an attempt to tie the Sunni clergy of the colonized peoples, including the Nokhchi, to a figure subordinate to the empire. The historian N. I. Pokrovsky wrote: "a broad project emerges for subordinating the entire mountain Sunni clergy to a special spiritual person"; the task set was "to turn the highlanders onto the true path, subordinate them to the Russian government, and destroy or hand over Shamil to us alive" (Shamil - imam, leader of the Dagestani and Chechen highlanders' resistance to the Russian conquest)(Citation: Кавказские войны и имамат Шамиля 2009). Only the establishment of the post, the appointment, and the preacher's years-long payment took place; subordinating the clergy did not succeed: "The preacher did not dare to show himself in the mountains"(Citation: Кавказские войны и имамат Шамиля 2009). The empire wound down the project only six years later: Golovin, who succeeded Rozen, agreed to release Mustafin based on a report by Minister of War Chernyshev of 13 November 1841 - "the teaching of Tajudin Effendi over the course of 6 years did not change the highlanders' attitude toward us in the slightest"(Citation: Кавказские войны и имамат Шамиля 2009).

On 31 July 1925 the Revolutionary Military Council of the USSR explained the operation being prepared by the properties of an entire people - the order says: "The Chechen oblast is a hotbed of criminal banditry spreading to the districts neighboring Chechnya... In their mass the Chechens are inclined to banditry as the main source of easy gain, which is furthered by the presence of a large quantity of weapons. Mountain Chechnya is a refuge for the most hardened enemies of Soviet power"(Citation: Хроника первого разоружения Чечни 2015). The label from the order passed into the operation's working nomenclature: the instruction of 4 August 1925, approved by Uborevich, commander of the North Caucasus Military District, Volodin, member of the district's Revolutionary Military Council, and Yevdokimov, plenipotentiary representative of the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB) for the krai, puts people in one row with rifles and "removes" them with a single verb - point 8 of the instruction reads: "If the conditions of the surrender of weapons are fulfilled, no house-to-house search is conducted, and only the bandit and vicious element is removed"(Citation: О подготовке к операции по разоружению и борьбе с бандитизмом в Чечне 2022). Thus criminality was declared a property of the people, and its men - an "element" subject to removal.

The Regular Army of the Russian Empire drove the population of the destroyed villages off their lands, which passed into the conqueror’s possession. Historian D. A. Khozhayev records that the inhabitants of the eight villages near Groznaya were “driven off the lands”(Citation: Чеченцы в Русско-Кавказской войне 1998). Imperial general Yermolov wrote to Emperor Alexander I that if the population refused to submit, they would be offered “to withdraw and join the other brigands,” and then “all the lands will remain at our disposal”(Citation: Чеченцы в Русско-Кавказской войне 1998).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers left Chechens without drinking water.
Russian pilots and artillerymen more than once destroyed substations and the water supply system in Grozny, the capital of Ichkeria, leaving the townspeople without water(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996)(Citation: Russian Federation/Northen Caucasus: Drinking water scarce in Grozny 1996).
Russian servicemen fired from armored personnel carriers and helicopters at Chechens who were going for water (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Russia: Three Months of War in Chechnya 1995)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).
On 31 January 1995, the occupiers shelled Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, from tanks and helicopters, leaving the Chechens in the village without water (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). In February 1995, Russian artillery shelled and aircraft bombed Argun, a town east of Grozny. Chechens in Argun hid in basements and went out for water only between seven and nine in the morning, while the crews of Russian helicopters fired at passers-by in the streets(Citation: Russia: Three Months of War in Chechnya 1995).
During the assault on Grozny in February 1995, Russian servicemen in the Katayama settlement within the city limits shot 28-year-old Dzhenchuraeva with the cannon of an armored personnel carrier as she was carrying water. Her brother tried to carry the body home and survived, although the occupiers wounded him in the shoulder. Lipkan Bazaeva, a teacher from Grozny and the wife of the murdered woman's cousin, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Prague in May 1996: "She went for water, believing that a woman would not be killed"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).
On 7 April 1995, the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) and OMON troops (police special forces) stormed Samashki. On 8 April, Russian soldiers searched houses in the village and set fire to most of them (see: "Total Destruction of Infrastructure"). On the morning of 8 April, Russian servicemen drove Yuzbek Shovkhalov, an elder of Samashki, into the basement of his house on Kooperativnaya Street, and the basement filled with smoke. In April 1995, the elder told the observer mission of Russian human rights organizations how he ran out of there with burns: "I run, thinking, at least there was a flask of water standing there. No, they had carried it out, they're drinking the water. They're all sitting on the other side of the street, sitting, laughing, cracking sunflower seeds"(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 10 April, a Chechen woman named Karnukaeva of Rabochaya Street told the mission about soldiers in the neighbors' yard, where she had hidden on 8 April: "They say to the old woman: 'Is this your drinking water?' She says: 'Yes, it's clean water.' 'Go on, you drink it first.' She took a mug, drank some water, then they drank themselves and spilled it, didn't leave a drop. They turned over all those barrels and flasks and poured out the water. In case anything happened, if there was a fire, so that no one could put it out. That's probably what they were thinking"(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995).
By 12 April 1995, Russian servicemen had shot through the water barrels in Samashki, and the Chechens in the village had nothing to keep water in(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996). The diary of a Memorial observer records on 14 April that the village was receiving no water, gas or electricity. That day, the command of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs eased entry into Samashki, and Kosov, an adviser to the president of Russian-controlled Ingushetia, organized the delivery of bread and water to the village(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995).
In the spring of 1996, a year after Russian troops captured Grozny, there was no water in the city's apartments, and there were two to three liters per person a day. The townspeople walked 5-10 kilometers for water and took it from the dirty Sunzha river, which flows through the city(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). In August 1996, Russian pilots bombed Grozny, and artillerymen shelled the city (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). A bulletin of the International Committee of the Red Cross of 2 September 1996 says that after these strikes all 80 thousand people in Grozny were left without drinking water, and at the end of August Red Cross engineers reached the city's only working pumping station and began distributing water, three liters per person a day(Citation: Russian Federation/Northen Caucasus: Drinking water scarce in Grozny 1996).
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

After capturing Alkhan-Yurt at the end of March 1919 the Volunteer Army for a month did not let the residents bury their dead - historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "As a punishment for the stubborn resistance, the White command for the course of a month did not permit the bodies of the village's fallen defenders to be committed to the earth"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers destroyed the museums, research institutes and ancient monuments of the Chechens.
During the storming of Grozny, Russian artillerymen shelled, and pilots bombed, the center of the city, where the museums and research institutes of Ichkeria stood(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Russian pilots fired rockets at ancient towers and settlements in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). The occupiers occupied the ruins of museums and looted what had survived (see: "Theft of Cultural Property")(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Russian troops burned almost the entire Central State Archive of the Chechen Republic and the republican libraries in Grozny (see: "Burning of Books and Archives")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Soldiers of the occupation troops destroyed mosques and leveled ancient burial mounds (see: "Destruction of Shrines and Necropolises")(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).
In January 1995, Russian troops destroyed the Chechen National Museum in Grozny. The museum held about 320 thousand exhibits, among them archaeological finds of the ancient and medieval Caucasus, traditional Chechen clothing and old manuscripts(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). The museum's director Isa Adayev told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Prague in May 1996: "From 1 to 4 January 1995, the museum building was shelled quite deliberately from several directions". When the director got to the museum on 7 January, "it was no longer a museum — nothing was left of it — only ruins". On 18 January, Russian special forces seized the ruins(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Khotin, deputy director of the museum center of the Russian Ministry of Culture, who inspected the ruins of the museum in late March 1995, told the public tribunal of the Glasnost Foundation in Moscow in February 1996: "The nature of the destruction shows that barrage fire was used there. Next to the museum there is a small park of about 50 fairly old trees. Well, all those trees are cut in half. All of them!"(Citation: Война в Чечне: Международный трибунал: Материалы опроса свидетелей: Первая сессия 1996).
In early 1995, the occupiers destroyed in Grozny the Research Institute of the Humanities of the Chechen Republic, founded in 1907(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). In 1995, Russian pilots fired rockets at and bombed Kogo-Maista, an old settlement in the mountains in the south of Ichkeria, far from the fighting. In the strikes, the occupiers destroyed six towers that had stood for thirteen centuries, killed the Chechen boy Deni Murtazov and wounded a woman of his family so badly that she became disabled(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997).
The human rights defenders of "Memorial" write that Russian troops destroyed or irreparably damaged in Grozny the university, the pedagogical and petroleum institutes, and the geological museum. In "Memorial's" assessment, Russian troops did not take the rescue of cultural property into account and inflicted irreparable damage on the culture of the Chechen people(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

The Russian Empire cut down the forests of the Nokhchi to strip their villages of natural protection and open a path for the troops. The imperial historian Potto writes that the “dense forest” stretching from the Argun to the Dzhalka, which served as “an obstacle to the destruction of the Germenchug fields and pastures,” was cut through in three days by a wide clearing “opening onto a large glade on which stood Germenchug and a multitude of auls”(Citation: Кавказская война. В 5 томах. Том 2. Ермоловское время 2007).

The introduction of the "blackboard" regime - a total economic blockade of settlements. The resolution of the Council of People's Commissars of the Ukrainian SSR and the CC of the CP(b)U of December 6, 1932, signed by Chubar and Kosior, prescribed "the immediate cessation of the delivery of goods, the complete cessation of cooperative and state trade on site, and the removal of all available goods from the respective cooperative and state shops," as well as "a complete ban on kolkhoz trade both for kolkhozes and kolkhoz members and for individual farmers"(Citation: О занесении на черную доску сел, злостно саботирующих хлебозаготовки 1932).

By the regulation of August 2, 1829, Commander-in-Chief Paskevich locked the Chechens' access to trade onto a commissar appointed by the empire: travel to imperial territory was permitted only with tickets (written passes) — "To him is also granted the right to issue tickets to the said Chechens for travel into our domains on trade business"(Citation: Акты собранные Кавказскою археографическою комиссиею. Том VII (1827-1831) 1878). In practice, the pass system was supplemented by arbitrariness: Chechen society wrote to Paskevich on November 21, 1829 that Engelhardt and Khasai-Musa "order their subordinates to place under arrest all those Chechens who come to them with tickets from Shahbaz," while those obedient to Khasai-Musa act so that the Chechens are deprived of their "means of sustenance"(Citation: Акты собранные Кавказскою археографическою комиссиею. Том VII (1827-1831) 1878).

Large-scale looting of state arsenals and the treasury during the punitive raid on the autonomy's capital: "Menshikov managed to remove part of the artillery"(Citation: Мазепа 2007)(Citation: Иван Мазепа и Российская империя. История «предательства» 2011); the remaining guns were blown up and the city burned.

Units of the Volunteer Army (the "Whites") captured the town of Fastiv in Kyiv province on 25 August 1919 (7 September by the modern calendar) - and on the same day began robbing the inhabitants of the town's Jewish quarters. Pakhomov, the Whites' temporary commandant, having received 25,000 roubles from a Jewish delegation, promised to take measures but refused to stop the violence at once, explaining why: "since the troops are greatly embittered against the Jews." The Whites' garrison was commanded by Belogortsev. The Whites killed on a schedule: "Towards evening all the Cossacks, regulars and partisans separately, were usually assembled for roll-call. After roll-call and prayer they scattered in groups across the town 'to work.'" Those fleeing were caught on the railway: "Many were taken off trains along the way and led into the forest to be shot"(Citation: Доклад Х. Гофмана о погромах в м. Фастов Киевской губ. 1919).
When a Russian delegation came to the commandant asking him to stop the pogrom, because the Russian population had begun to suffer from it too, he asked: "And who is doing the robbing?" - and, on hearing that the Russian population was also taking part, replied: "And later they will say it was the Cossacks who robbed"(Citation: Доклад Х. Гофмана о погромах в м. Фастов Киевской губ. 1919). On 23 September 1919 Kundo, the Whites' commandant in Fastiv, issued order No. 2 declaring everything settled: "I add that measures for the protection of order in the townlet were taken long ago, all apprehensions are entirely groundless. Of all cases of robbery, violence and requisitions I request immediate notification to the commandant's office"(Citation: Приказ военной комендатуры ВСЮР в м. Фастов Киевской губ. № 2 1919).
Rabinovich, a commissioner of the Russian Red Cross, described the result of the three days thus: "The pogrom, like a tornado, destroyed, burned and scattered the greater half of the town... From the smouldering ruins of the fires bodies of those burned in the houses were still being recovered"(Citation: Сообщение Г. И. Рабиновича о последствиях погрома в м. Фастов 1919). By 30 September 1919, 600 killed, 100 burned and 315 wounded had been counted in Fastiv - out of eight thousand Jewish inhabitants of the town, and the figure was incomplete: "there are far more killed, since to this day bodies are being found in the woods"(Citation: Доклад Х. Гофмана о погромах в м. Фастов Киевской губ. 1919).

Total massacre of the civilian population: "Funck slaughtered more than a thousand people in the small town of Terey (Tereyska sloboda) and burned the town down, and also burned Dryhalov (Nedryhailiv)… and ordered everyone encountered to be killed, so as to instill horror in others"(Citation: Сочинения в 12 томах. Том 10 1959). "In total, about 15 thousand Ukrainians died in the Baturyn tragedy, including all the women and children"(Citation: Мазепа 2007)(Citation: Иван Мазепа и Российская империя. История «предательства» 2011).

On 26 May 1919, at the height of the uprising of Ukrainian peasants under Hryhoriv against the Soviet authority, Lenin, head of the RSFSR government, telegraphed to Kyiv to Rakovsky, head of the colonial administration of Ukraine (the UkrSSR), and to Kharkiv to Mezhlauk, its deputy war minister: "Decree and carry into effect the complete disarming of the population, shoot on the spot mercilessly for any concealed rifle. The whole crux of the moment: a quick victory in the Donbas, the collection of all rifles from the villages, the creation of a solid army"; he ordered the telegram read "to all prominent Bolsheviks"(Citation: Телеграмма В. И. Ленина Х. Г. Раковскому и В. И. Межлауку 1919). A day earlier Antonov-Ovseenko, commander of the RSFSR's Ukrainian Front, had ordered the armies "to disarm the local population" in their areas of operation(Citation: Приказ армиям Украинского фронта № 68 о ликвидации авантюры Григорьева 1919).
In secret order No. 579 of 11 December 1919 Trotsky, war minister of the RSFSR, named the goal in a single clause - "the unconditional and universal disarming of the village population" of Ukraine was declared "the basic condition of success"(Citation: Приказ Реввоенсовета Республики № 579 о мерах по борьбе с партизанщиной в Красной Армии 1919).
On 26 July 1919 Skrypnyk, plenipotentiary of the same administration's Defence Council, telegraphed on the course of the disarmament from the Trypillia district: "The disarming of the population is carried out by searches; all those guilty of concealing weapons and war materiel are handed over to the field revtribunal [the Bolsheviks' military court]"(Citation: Телеграмма Н. А. Скрыпника о ликвидации банд Зеленого 1919).
In the village of Tiutkovychi in Rivne district on 6 July 1919 an assembly of village representatives, in the presence of Soviet military commissar Senichkin, resolved to surrender "rifles, machine guns, cartridges" and asked "to leave the population 15 rifles and cartridges for the defence of the population against bandits"; in the same protocol the assembly complained that Soviet soldiers were taking property arbitrarily, without a warrant(Citation: Протокол заседания представителей уездных органов Советской власти в д. Тютьковичи 1919).

The dispatch of Cossack regiments to distant theaters of war (the Baltic lands, Poland), which led to their exhaustion. The troops were "wearied by year-round military service, impoverished, dismounted, destitute"(Citation: Иван Мазепа и Российская империя. История «предательства» 2011)(Citation: Мазепа 2007).

Suppressing the uprising of 1840, the empire demanded of the Chechens a public renunciation of resistance. General Grabbe, commander of the troops of the Caucasus Line (the chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), in an appeal to the insurgents of 14 June 1840 demanded repentance: "Come to your senses and save yourselves now by sincere repentance and immediate submission" ("submission" - the imperial formula of subordination)(Citation: Движение горцев северо-восточного Кавказа в 20-50 гг. XIX века: сборник документов 1959). The next day, 15 June 1840, he issued the "Conditions prescribed to submitting highlanders", whose point 8 prescribed that the insurgent auls "renounce all participation in the pernicious teaching of Shamil" (Shamil - the imam, leader of the resistance of the highlanders of Dagestan and Chechnya to the Russian conquest; "pernicious teaching" - the imperial label for muridism, the religious movement of the resistance)(Citation: Движение горцев северо-восточного Кавказа в 20-50 гг. XIX века: сборник документов 1959).

The Regular Army of the Russian Empire, having moved troops onto the Sunzha and occupied Chechen land, demanded that the elders of Chechen villages renew their oath of submission under threat of reprisal as against “open enemies.” Imperial general Yermolov testifies in his “Notes” that in May 1818 “the elders of almost all the principal Chechen villages were summoned to me,” to the military camp, and he demanded “that henceforth such [depredations] no longer be committed, and in confirmation they must renew their old oath of submission and return the captives held by them”(Citation: Записки А.П. Ермолова. 1798-1826 гг. 1991). The demand went unfulfilled: the elders “promised nothing”(Citation: Записки А.П. Ермолова. 1798-1826 гг. 1991).

The "Conditions prescribed to submitting highlanders", issued by general Grabbe, commander of the troops of the Caucasus Line (the chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), on 15 June 1840, obliged the Chechen auls to refuse shelter to members of the resistance and to hand over people who had escaped the empire's power. Point 8 prescribed: "Not to give refuge in their auls to abreks, murids and unsubdued highlanders" (abrek - the imperial label for a highlander declared an outlaw; murids - the imam's disciples and warriors); point 11: "To hand over all Russian prisoners and runaways staying in the mountains" - by runaways the empire meant its own soldiers and serfs who had gone over to the highlanders(Citation: Движение горцев северо-восточного Кавказа в 20-50 гг. XIX века: сборник документов 1959). Handovers went on even before the decree, under the pressure of the winter expeditions: the imperial historian Yurov recorded of the outcome of the December 1839 march of general Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line, through Lesser Chechnya (the lowland-piedmont western part of Chechnya): "97 abreks, 7 prisoners and two runaways were handed over", and of the January 1840 march along the Michik river - the auls "handed over 30 abreks"(Citation: 1840, 1841 и 1842-й годы на Кавказе 1886).

The Regular Army of the Russian Empire held representatives of the villages along the Sunzha as a pledge of submission. Imperial general Yermolov testifies in his “Notes” that when the troops advanced to the Sunzha, “amanats (hostages) from their villages were taken into the camp”(Citation: Записки А.П. Ермолова. 1798-1826 гг. 1991). Imperial historian Potto confirms that Yermolov “took amanats from all the auls sitting along the Sunzha”(Citation: Кавказская война. В 5 томах. Том 2. Ермоловское время 2007).

After forcing the signing of the treaty, Moscow moved to the direct occupation of the autonomy's living space. The articles codified the expansion of the military presence: "besides Kyiv, tsarist voivodes were introduced into Pereiaslav, Chernihiv, Nizhyn, Bratslav, and Uman"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 8 2011) – garrisons headed by voivodes ensured physical control over the territory from within.

On 31 July 1925 the Revolutionary Military Council of the USSR, in the order justifying the operation to disarm Chechnya, declared the Chechens incapable of proper farming: "The rich lands granted to the Chechens on the plain after the revolution are not used by them in full; they run their agriculture in backward forms, are not industrious"(Citation: Хроника первого разоружения Чечни 2015). The accusation stands in a military order as one of the grounds for sending in troops: the lands were "granted" to the people by the authorities themselves, their way of farming was declared backward by the same authorities, and the conclusion drawn from this assessment was a military operation. Historian T. U. Elbuzdukayeva, who publishes the order, also cites its continuation: "political indications" had ripened - the population's weariness of war and the demand to fight "banditry"(Citation: Хроника первого разоружения Чечни 2015) - that is, even by the document's own logic the war was to be waged not on economic backwardness, yet it is backwardness that is set down as a justification.

In 1830, during an ongoing earthquake, General Rozen 4th, who commanded the troops on the left flank of the Caucasus Line (the eastern section of the empire's fortified border along the Terek and Sunzha rivers), on the orders of commander-in-chief Paskevich sent proclamations out to the auls, instilling in the people an artificial picture of the world: the natural disaster was declared God's punishment for resisting the empire. The historian Ya. Z. Akhmadov wrote about how this lie sounded among the Nokhchi: “supporters of the Russian orientation claimed that the earthquake was caused by the wrath of Allah over the attempt at an armed uprising”(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005). The imperial historian Volkonsky acknowledges the source of the suggestion: the commander-in-chief “ordered General Rozen 4th to spread entirely opposite rumors among the people, namely, that the earthquake had been sent down by God upon the Mountain Peoples for their ill-intentioned acts against the Russian government”(Citation: Война на Восточном Кавказе с 1824 по 1834 г. в связи с мюридизмом 1886). The imperial historian Potto recorded the act: Rozen “resorted to proclamations in which he sought to assure the people that the earthquake had been sent down upon them as punishment for their treason and their ill-intentioned acts against the Russian government”(Citation: Кавказская война. В 5 томах. Том 5. Время Паскевича, или Бунт Чечни 2006).

The targets of the artillery and aviation were often not military objectives but inhabited settlements as such: the instruction of 4 August 1925, approved by Uborevich, commander of the North Caucasus Military District, Volodin, member of the district's Revolutionary Military Council, and Yevdokimov, plenipotentiary representative of the OGPU (the political police, a predecessor of today's FSB) for the krai, prescribed - "If the population of the aul does not fulfil the demand to surrender weapons in the established time in full, or fulfils it partially, the detachment command, by way of threat, opens artillery fire (or, in the absence of artillery, machine-gun fire) for 10 minutes with high bursts and half-strikes", and added: "depending on the situation the warning fire, as a measure of influence, may be opened several times as well"(Citation: О подготовке к операции по разоружению и борьбе с бандитизмом в Чечне 2022); the document names no military objective and no target inside the village at all. Of the 242 disarmed settlements 101 came under rifle, machine-gun and artillery fire, 16 under strikes from the air(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005); by the count of historian E. F. Zhupikova, "104 one-pud bombs [about 1.7 tonnes] were dropped on the 16 auls where the leaders of the insurgents were hiding"(Citation: К вопросу о разоружении Чечни в 1920-1925 годах 1998). A one-pud aerial bomb is about 16 kilograms, the weight of a round of a modern 120 mm mortar; on average six to seven such bombs fell per aul. The aviation was directed by Petrozhitsky, chief of the district's air force, and historian T. U. Elbuzdukayeva lists the targets by name: "In the course of the operation the aircraft of the 3rd, and from 6 September also of the 5th aviation detachments delivered air strikes on the auls of Zumsoy, Dai, Tagir Khoy, Akki Bougi, Oshni, Khimoy, Nizheloy, Ragekhoy, Urus-Martan and Nozhay-Yurt"(Citation: Хроника первого разоружения Чечни 2015). What the "warning fire" looked like in a single aul can be seen from the dispatch on Achkhoy-Martan of 25 August 1925: "15 shrapnel rounds were fired at the aul, first four with a high burst, then to strike. After two Chechen women had been wounded, the inhabitants began to hand over their weapons"(Citation: Из архива Дахо Джанхотова: ведомость приема-передачи уголовных дел как исторический документ 2021). Historian A. Yu. Lashkov writes of the strike on the aul of Dai: "Initially, because of heavy fog, the neighboring settlement of Chubakhkimeroy was mistakenly subjected to the air strike"(Citation: 1925 год: спецоперация Красной армии 2000).

In the autumn of 1994, Russia attacked the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria under the name of a puppet opposition, and on 11 December 1994 the Russian army openly invaded the republic. The occupiers bombed Chechen television, jammed journalists' satellite links and kept them away from the sites of their strikes.
Commanders of the occupation forces ordered that journalists not be let into the sites of assaults and bombings. The Russian military and police at checkpoints did not let journalists, including those with accreditation from the Russian government, into the villages and towns that Russian troops were striking (see: "Censorship")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Human rights defenders of the American Committee to Protect Journalists write that Russian troops in Ichkeria jammed journalists' satellite transmissions, exposed their film and destroyed their equipment(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1996: Russia 1997).
On 29 November 1994, Russia announced that at 2 p.m. it would cut off all communications with Ichkeria(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-94-229) 1994). From 21 to 24 December, Russian pilots struck the television center in Grozny. Deinekin, commander of Russian military aviation, named the aim of these strikes: "to stop the rabid anti-Russian propaganda"(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
On 3 January 1995, Russian pilots bombed Shali, a town southeast of Grozny. Human rights defenders of Human Rights Watch write that the pilots were apparently trying to hit a radio communication tower, but killed several townspeople at the market and in the hospital (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Russia: Three Months of War in Chechnya 1995). On 7 and 8 April, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs (predecessors of today's Rosgvardia) stormed Samashki, a village in the west of Ichkeria, and killed 103 Chechen civilians there (see: "Mass Killings of Civilians")(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 11 April, the occupiers at the post near the village did not let journalists in and admitted them only on 13 April(Citation: Трагедия села Самашки. Чечня. Апрель 1995. Дневник правозащитника 1995)(Citation: Всеми имеющимися средствами… Результаты независимого расследования Наблюдательной миссии правозащитных общественных организаций в зоне вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1995). On 8 October, Russian pilots bombed Roshni-Chu, a village southwest of Grozny (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The occupiers blocked all the roads to the village, and men of the police special forces from the Russian city of Irkutsk at the post did not let journalists in, citing an order(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010)(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-95-198) 1995). From 11 December, before the "elections" of the head of the puppet government on 14-17 December, Russian soldiers at checkpoints did not let journalists without special passes into Grozny (see: "Sham Expression of Popular Will")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 14 to 20 December, after the Armed Forces of Ichkeria had liberated Gudermes, the second-largest city of the republic, the occupiers shelled and bombed the city, and until 25 December did not let the press in (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996).
In January 1996, the command of the occupation forces closed Grozny and the east of Ichkeria to the press(Citation: Caught in the Crossfire: Civilians in Gudermes and Pervomayskoye 1996). From February until the first days of March, the occupiers shelled with artillery the encircled settlement of Novogroznensky in the east of Ichkeria and the villages of Alleroy, Tsentoroy, Bachi-Yurt and Suvorov-Yurt (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). The Russian military did not let journalists in there(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 3 to 9 March, Russian troops shelled Sernovodsk, a village in the west of Ichkeria, with artillery and fired on it from helicopters (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). From 6 to 9 March, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were attacking the occupiers in Grozny, Russian officials did not let journalists into the city(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1996: Russia 1997). On 10 March, the Russian military commandant of Sernovodsk forbade letting journalists, human rights defenders and any foreigners into the village (see: "Expulsion of Foreign Missions")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
On 15 March 1996, the Internal Troops of Russia's Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Russian 58th Army began the assault on Samashki (see: "Military Intervention")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Sources differ on the number of Chechen civilians the occupiers killed in the village during the assault: 35 according to the villagers' list(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010) or about 600 according to a doctor who treated people there (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks")(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999)(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). On 17 and 18 March, the occupiers did not let independent journalists from Moscow through to the village. Maria Eismont, a correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Segodnya, told the public tribunal of the Russian Glasnost Foundation in Moscow on 22 April that on 26 and 27 March the Russian military stopped her on the roads to Samashki, and that she got into the village five days later. In Sernovodsk, Russian soldiers who had taken part in the assault turned the journalists back with the words: "There's no need to go there, there's nothing for you to do there, all the more so since there is nothing at all left to look at." Alexander Trushin, a correspondent of the Moscow newspaper Obshchaya Gazeta, told the Glasnost tribunal on 21 April that in early April the chief of the Russian checkpoint near the village phoned a general and did not let the journalists through: "I asked the captain: 'Did you report why we are going, for what purpose?' He answered: 'Yes, the general knows, and nevertheless the order is not to let you through'"(Citation: Материалы опроса свидетелей. Вторая сессия. Москва, 20-24 апреля 1996 года. Дополнительные слушания. Третья сессия. Прага, 24-26 мая 1996 года 1997). Human rights defenders of Memorial write that reports of this assault did not reach television and radio(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
On 21 April 1996, the occupiers killed Dzhokhar Dudayev, the president of Ichkeria, during his conversation on a satellite phone with a mediator in the peace talks; according to the version that human rights defenders of Memorial consider likely, the Russian military located the signal of this phone (see: "Neutralization of the Opposition")(Citation: Daily Report: Central Eurasia (FBIS-SOV-96-080) 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). On 8 August 1996, while the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were liberating Grozny, Russian soldiers did not let four journalists of foreign media into the city through either of its two entrances(Citation: Attacks on the Press in 1996: Russia 1997).
Human rights defenders of Memorial write that in the second year of the war Russian troops cut off from the press the areas they deemed undesirable far more tightly and successfully than in the first year(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).

Removing Cossack regiments from the Cossack hierarchy and placing them under the direct command of imperial officials: Peter I handed the direction of the Ladoga Canal works to B.-C. Münnich, who "took over from Prince A. Menshikov the direction of the construction (digging) of the Ladoga Canal"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 6 2009); Cossack corps were dispatched to these works "by order of Tsar Peter I"(Citation: Енциклопедія історії України: Т. 8 2011).

The forced use of Cossacks to build imperial infrastructure under harsh conditions: "in the making of fortifications around the Kyiv-Pechersk Monastery"(Citation: Иван Мазепа и Российская империя. История «предательства» 2011)(Citation: Мазепа 2007).

The amanat-and-tribute system of Pullo, commander of the left flank of the Caucasus Line (a chain of imperial fortifications on the land of the Nokhchi), created within Chechen society a privileged layer with power over its compatriots. The offices of the overseers appointed by the empire over the auls (the pristavs) were handed by the empire to Chechens themselves: the imperial historian Yurov writes that the pristavs "were chosen predominantly, if not exclusively, from among the militiamen" - from the highland militia, armed units of highlanders in the empire's service(Citation: 1840, 1841 и 1842-й годы на Кавказе 1886). The historian N. I. Pokrovsky showed the mechanics of the split: the office of pristav was unpaid, so only "certain representatives of strong families" could take it, and they "took advantage of the opportunity to use their power for further accumulation"; "by creating in Chechnya a local administration, Chechen by nationality, tsarism hoped to create at the same time the Chechen 'aristocracy' it so needed"(Citation: Кавказские войны и имамат Шамиля 2009). The empire gave part of the society power and privileges over the rest and bound this layer to itself, not to the people: the handing of offices to the "strong families" is documented; the calculation of growing a loyal "aristocracy" was formulated by the historian N. I. Pokrovsky.

On 22 January (4 February) 1918, five days before the seizure of Kyiv, Muravyov (commander of the Soviet troops acting against the Central Rada of Ukraine) signed order No. 9 at Darnytsia station near Kyiv: "I order the troops of both armies to mercilessly destroy in Kyiv all officers and cadets, Haidamaks, monarchists and all enemies of the revolution. Units that kept neutrality must be immediately disbanded, their property handed over to the Military Revolutionary Committee of the city of Kyiv"(Citation: Приказ М. А. Муравьева о задачах армии по обороне Киева после его освобождения 1918). Antonov-Ovseyenko (who commanded the whole expedition into Ukraine) printed this order in his notes together with a reproduction of Muravyov's handwritten original and wrote that the order "at once, by its tone and by its instruction on summary reprisal against all suspicious persons, alarmed our party organization and the Soviet authorities"(Citation: Записки о гражданской войне. Т. 1 1924). On 28 January (10 February) the Kyiv Soviet of Workers' and Soldiers' Deputies (the organ of that very Soviet power which the troops had brought) resolved: "The Soviet expresses its resolute condemnation of the unceasing lynchings of prisoners, which stain the glorious victory of the proletariat. Those who have disgraced themselves by the murder of the unarmed must be expelled from the ranks of the socialist army and handed over to a revolutionary court. Enough violence!"(Citation: Заседание Совета Р. и С. Д. 28 января 1918). On 19 March 1918 members of the committee of the 1st revolutionary army came with a complaint against Muravyov to Dzerzhinsky, head of the Cheka, the Bolsheviks' secret police(Citation: Слідча справа М.А.Муравйова: Документована історія 2001). On 5 May Dzerzhinsky testified to the investigative commission: "our worst enemy could not have done us as much harm as he did with his nightmarish reprisals, executions, tyranny, and by granting the soldiers the right to plunder towns and villages. All this he did in the name of our Soviet power, turning the whole population against us. Plunder and violence — that was his deliberate military tactic"(Citation: Слідча справа М.А.Муравйова: Документована історія 2001). On 15 March 1996, in Samashki, Russian soldiers led two elderly Chechens, the owner of a house on Vygonnaya Street and his neighbor, out of the house, put them on top of an armored vehicle and drove them around under bullets for six or seven hours. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996).
On 10 August 1996, when the Armed Forces of Ichkeria were liberating Grozny, soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs searched City Hospital No. 9 in Grozny. For two days, the occupiers held about 500 patients, their relatives, doctors and nurses hostage (see: "Hostage-Taking"). Movsar Tembulatov, the deputy chief physician, told the human rights defenders of "Memorial" and Human Rights Watch in the hospital on 13 October 1996 how Russian soldiers went down into the basement: "they put me or one of the other doctors in front as some kind of cover, with a submachine gunner behind"(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
On 12 August 1996, soldiers of the army of Ichkeria repelled an attack by Russian troops trying to break through to the occupiers encircled in the hospital. The commander of the Russian servicemen in the hospital agreed to lead his soldiers out in exchange for captives and demanded 100 doctors, nurses, walking patients and their relatives as a human shield for himself. Khadis Malsagov, one of the hostages, told the human rights defenders of "Memorial" on 24 August 1996: "As soon as everyone had moved away from the hospital, they [the Russian soldiers] line the women up and say they will shoot them if the captives are not handed over to them immediately". The soldiers of Khizir Khachukayev handed over all the captives. At the gates of their base, the occupiers released the people from the human shield. When the people were returning to the hospital, Russian troops fired several dozen mortar shells at it, killed the nurse Toita Kutukhanova and wounded two nurses, two doctors and a woman patient (see: "Indiscriminate Attacks"). On the evening of 12 August and the morning of 13 August, the patients and medics left the hospital for the building of the International Committee of the Red Cross nearby(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
On 12 August 1996, soldiers of the 101st Brigade of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs took men from the blocks of Grozny around the "15th Gorodok", their base on Lenin Street, and shielded themselves with them on the way there (see: "Hostage-Taking")(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010). Two of them, a father and son, the occupiers tied with wire to an armored personnel carrier, drove under fire to Khankala, the main base of the occupation troops on the eastern outskirts of the city, and released on 16 August(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996).
The 1996 report of "Memorial" says that Russian servicemen and officers of Russian agencies in Ichkeria systematically took hostages and shielded themselves with human shields. According to the report, the occupiers shielded themselves with Chechens during the last six months of the war, from March to August 1996, most often the soldiers of the Internal Troops of the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs(Citation: За спинами мирных жителей. Захват заложников и использование гражданского населения в качестве «живого щита» федеральными войсками России в ходе вооруженного конфликта в Чечне 1996).
The prosecutors of the Russian army did not investigate how Russian troops shielded themselves with Chechens during assaults and held no one accountable for it (see: "Impunity of Perpetrators")(Citation: Russia/Chechnya: A Legacy of Abuse 1997)(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
In August 1996, the Armed Forces of Ichkeria liberated Grozny from the occupiers, forcing Russia to the negotiating table(Citation: The War in Chechnya 1999). On 31 August 1996, peace agreements were signed in Khasavyurt (see: "Sham Treaties")(Citation: Хасавюртовские соглашения 1996). On 31 December 1996, the last Russian troops left the republic(Citation: Россия - Чечня - цепь ошибок и преступлений. 1994—1996 2010).
